subject: Multivariate log-normal responses and effect sizes

messages.author: cc9c33c996d6abc6
messages.subject: Multivariate log-normal responses and effect sizes
parts:
Hello dear brms users,

I am trying to fit a brm model with multiple (four) lognormal-distributed response variables, and I would like to solicit your advice on several points. The model I have fitted has the following form:

model1 <- brm(
    formula = cbind(log(resp1), log(resp2), log(resp3), log(resp4)) ~ 1 + predictor1,
    data = data, family = gaussian(),
    prior = prior,
    warmup = 1000, thin = 10, iter = 10000,
    chains = 2, cores = parallel::detectCores(),

    control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95)
    )

Basically, my idea was to log-transform these variables in order to be able to fit a gaussian multivariate brm model but I know this is a debatable choice (and it makes the interpretation of the posterior distribution in the log scale much less easy). Would anyone have alternative approach to suggest ?

Additionally, I was wondering how the effect sizes computations detailed in Gelman & Pardoe (2006) or Marsman et al. (2017) would be directly applicable in my case (i.e., a multivariate case) ? Is it possible to compute an estimate of the effect of predictor1 on a multivariate 'mixture' of the four response variables and / or on each response variable independently ?

Do not hesitate to redirect me toward external ressources (books, articles, forum topics, etc).

Best,

Ladislas

Gelman & Pardoe (2006):  - http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/rsquared.pdf
Marsman et al. (2017) - http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/birdseye.pdf (https://osf.io/3e5vh/)

messages.author: 6e3dd74b422c061b
messages.subject: Re: Multivariate log-normal responses and effect sizes
parts:
Hi Ladislas,

unfortunately, brms is not yet very flexible when it comes to multivariate models, but I am working on a way more general implementation within brms.
One other package that is currently more flexible for multivariate models is MCMCglmm, but I am not sure if it satisfies your needs since it doesn't support the lognormal distribution either.

I don't see any obstacles to applying the mentioned effect sizes independently to each response. The only difference between multiple separate gaussian models and one multivarite gaussian model is the estimation of the residual correlation matrix. Since brms fits separate coefficients for each response, you should have everthing available to compute the effect sizes separately.
I am not sure how one would compute a single effect size across responses, but I am admittedly not an expert in this regard.

Best
Paul

messages.author: 6e3dd74b422c061b
messages.subject: Re: Multivariate log-normal responses and effect sizes
parts:
For one-sided hypothesis (e.g. x > 0), we get Inf, if all posterior samples of x are above zero. In this case, we have infinitely more posterior mass (as measured by posterior samples) above zero than below.

The only way to get a non-inf value in this case would be to approximate the histogram of the posterior samples with a smooth density, but this is not really what I would recommend doing.
Or you could run many more samples in the hope that some of them eventually fall below zero.

In such a case one might simply want to say that x > 0 is over 1000 (or more) times more likely than x <= 0.
